title: The 442nd leaves the Vosges

facts.text: On 17 November 1944 the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, the Army's Japanese American regiment, pulled back to Docelles and was released from the 36th Infantry Division after more than a month of fighting in the Vosges Mountains of eastern France.
In October the regiment had liberated Bruyeres, taken Biffontaine, and from 26 to 30 October fought through the forest to rescue the 211 surviving men of the 141st Infantry's Lost Battalion.

The cost was enormous. The regiment's journal counts 140 killed and 1,800 other casualties in the Vosges, including wounded, sick and trench foot cases. Other accounts give more than 800 casualties between 14 and 31 October alone.
By 8 November Company I had no officers left and was commanded by a corporal promoted on the spot, T/5 Clarence Taba. Company K had 17 riflemen, led by a sergeant.

On 12 November Maj. Gen. John Dahlquist of the 36th Division held a formation to present citations. Seeing so few men, he demanded to know why the whole regiment was not there. The acting commander, Lt. Col. Virgil Miller, answered that this was all that was left. The exact words differ between accounts.
The next morning, 13 November, the regiment went back into the line in the snow covered forest overlooking the Taintrux valley, which leads to St Die, holding positions and sending out patrols.

Shelling and patrol fights went on. On 15 November the 81 mm mortars of Company H silenced two German machine gun nests, and German troops set fire to St Die and Corcieux; the glow lit the night sky for miles.
At Docelles the men finally got hot showers, and 382 new Japanese American replacements joined the regiment.
On 19 November the combat team left the Vosges by truck. Three days and 540 miles later it reached St Jeannet near Nice, to hold the French and Italian border in the Maritime Alps.
The men called the months on the Riviera front the Champagne Campaign. It was quieter than the Vosges, but not safe: shelling, mines and patrols still took lives.

photoNote: US Army Signal Corps photo dated 12 November 1944: color guards and color bearers of the 442nd Combat Team stand at attention in snow while citations are read, the regiment's thin ranks behind them. This is the Dahlquist formation itself. NARA 111-SC-196716-S (naId 100310394), use Unrestricted, public domain. 1920 x 1528 from the 2877 px scan. Strong faces; frame on the four men in front. Number 196716-S is bottom left. Caution: NARA 111-SC-185158, catalogued as F Company near St Die 13 Nov 1944, actually shows Nisei soldiers in a jeep in a US training camp; do not use it as a Vosges photo.
photoCredit: Color guards of the 442nd Combat Team stand at attention as citations are read, France, 12 November 1944. NARA 111-SC-196716-S, public domain.

declassified.fact: Pfc. Joe Nishimoto of Company G, from Fresno, California, crept forward alone through a mined and booby trapped area near La Houssiere on 7 November 1944 and knocked out German machine gun positions holding up his company. Days later, in the regiment's last week in the Vosges, he was killed; the regiment's journal lists him on 14 November. His Distinguished Service Cross was upgraded to the Medal of Honor in 2000.

body:
A general asked why the whole regiment had not turned out for his ceremony. He was told that it had.

17 November 1944. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, the Army's Japanese American regiment, pulled back to Docelles and was released from the 36th Infantry Division after more than a month in the Vosges Mountains of eastern France.

In October the regiment freed Bruyeres, took Biffontaine, and broke through to the 211 surviving men of the 141st Infantry's Lost Battalion. Its own journal counts 140 killed and 1,800 other casualties in the Vosges.

By 8 November Company I had no officers left and was led by a corporal promoted on the spot, T/5 Clarence Taba. Company K was down to 17 riflemen. When Maj. Gen. John Dahlquist reviewed the regiment on 12 November, the acting commander, Lt. Col. Virgil Miller, told him this was all that was left. Accounts differ on his exact words.

At Docelles the men finally got hot showers, and 382 new Japanese American replacements arrived. On 19 November trucks carried them 540 miles south to the French and Italian border.
